name: A Guide to Good Recording
category: Recording and the words we use
headline: Someone is going to read this. Write it for them.
intro: Training that helps your team write records for the child who may read them at 25.

problem.question: Bethany is 24, and this is all her file says about the week she was moved.
with: What you saw, heard and think kept apart
Chronologies that show the impact on the child
Notes and reports written to the child
problem.standards: UCL's MIRRA research with care-experienced adults found gaps in how their childhood records were kept, and how hard they were to access.
problem.evidence: What changes practice is working on real notes with one model. Bring your own anonymised notes if you can.

groups: Social workers, senior practitioners and team managers
Fostering, adoption, early help and family support
Personal advisers and leaving care workers
Residential staff, independent reviewing officers and business support
notes: Anyone who writes in a child's record
One team or a mixed group

outcomes: Read it as the child would
Describe what it is like for a care-experienced adult to read their childhood file.
Recognise how one vague note can give three readers three different pictures of a child.
Use Munro's research to explain why separating fact, what was said and opinion matters.
Explain cumulative harm, and why a chronology must record the impact on the child.
Use "What do I think, why, and what should I do?" and build an event, impact, action chronology.
Write a note or report addressed to the child, replacing labels with what happened and what they said.

pillars.title: Four things every good record does
pillars.stance: Someone is going to read this
pillars.stance_line: The next worker, a manager, an inspector, and often the child, years later.
items: What I saw, what I was told and what I think, each made clear.
What do I think, why, and what should I do?
A chronology of event, impact on the child and action taken.
Written to the child as "you", in words they would recognise.
pillars.base: Drawing on UCL's MIRRA project, Eileen Munro on reasoning, Bromfield, Gillingham and Higgins on cumulative harm, and Writing to the Child.

story_line: Four stories run through the day: Bethany, 24, Ethan, 7, Lily, 12, and Kieran, 10. Each is a composite, drawn from real experiences of care.

sections: What I saw, heard and think

phone.title: What I saw, heard and think
phone.intro: Sort one home visit note into three columns.
fields: Two plates on the table. Ethan in school uniform at 4pm.
Mum said she hadn't slept since the letter came.
Mum is under strain. I want to check support.
Her words and the letter. Call family support tomorrow.
phone.key: Keep what you saw, heard and think apart, so your reasoning can be tested.

facilitator.name: Luke Rodgers BEM
facilitator.line: From care leaver to care leader
paras: Luke went into care at 10. He has spent his career inside children's services as a consultant, trainer and keynote speaker, and is CEO of The Care Leaders.
He has trained staff across health, social care and education nationally, including Staffordshire, where four organisations trained 400 staff together.
He led the national engagement on England's new fostering standards for the Department for Education, so he knows what the standards expect of the adults around a child.
He was a Knowledge Equity Fellow at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, and was awarded the British Empire Medal in 2018 for commitment to children and families.
